schema_name: Clearnet Networking — Full Detail Knowledge Graph

topic.summary: A machine-readable knowledge graph covering clearnet terminology, its relationship to the Internet and World Wide Web, surface/deep/dark web distinctions, search indexing, IP-address exposure, anonymity networks, privacy considerations, technical context, and source provenance.

provenance.primary_input: User-supplied text of Wikipedia article Clearnet (networking)

limitations: The supplied Wikipedia page is marked as a stub and provides limited technical detail.
The three references in the supplied article are historical, so they should not be treated as current operational-security guidance.
An IP address does not by itself prove the identity of a natural person.
Clearnet is used inconsistently: broad usage refers to the public Internet, while narrow usage refers to the indexed surface web.

entities.name: Clearnet
entities.description: A term typically referring to the publicly accessible Internet; sometimes used as a synonym for the surface web.

attributes.usage_variation: Broad usage means publicly accessible Internet; narrower usage means indexed surface web.
attributes.anonymity: Ordinary clearnet browsing is not inherently anonymous.

entities.name: Internet
entities.description: Global network infrastructure supporting distributed services and applications.

entities.name: World Wide Web
entities.description: A distributed information service operating over the Internet; it is not synonymous with the Internet.

entities.name: Surface web
entities.description: Web content indexed and retrievable through traditional search engines.

attributes.caveat: Indexability is not the same as public accessibility.

entities.name: Deep web
entities.description: Content not indexed by conventional search engines, whether or not it is publicly accessible.

examples: interactive sites requiring additional user input

entities.name: Darknet
entities.description: A network or set of services commonly reached using specialized software or configurations and often associated with anonymity networks.

entities.name: Dark web
entities.description: Web content or services hosted on darknets or anonymity networks; not synonymous with all deep-web content.

entities.name: Tor
entities.description: An anonymity network that routes traffic through relays to reduce the ability to link users to destinations.

limits: endpoint compromise, account logins, misconfiguration, and traffic correlation can affect privacy

entities.name: Anonymity service
entities.description: A service or network intended to reduce linkability between a user, their network address, and their destination.

entities.name: IP address
entities.description: A network-layer address used for Internet Protocol communication.

attributes.privacy_caveat: An observed address may identify a shared gateway, proxy, VPN, carrier NAT, or network endpoint rather than a particular person.

entities.name: Client-transmitted data and metadata
entities.description: Data sent or exposed during client-server communication, potentially including request headers, cookies, browser characteristics, and account identifiers.

entities.name: Website
entities.description: A collection of related web resources served by a web server or application infrastructure.

entities.name: Traditional search engine
entities.description: A system that collects web content, creates an index, and retrieves ranked results in response to queries.

entities.name: Search-engine indexing
entities.description: Representing collected content in a searchable index; crawling and indexing are distinct processes and not all content is indexed.

entities.name: Public accessibility
entities.description: The ability to reach a resource without specialized network membership or credentials.

entities.name: Online privacy
entities.description: The ability to limit collection, linkage, retention, and disclosure of information about online activity.

entities.name: Encryption in transit
entities.description: Cryptographic protection of data while it travels between endpoints; encryption does not by itself provide anonymity.

entities.name: Proxy server
entities.description: An intermediary that makes requests to destinations on behalf of a client.

entities.name: Virtual private network (VPN)
entities.description: A technology that tunnels traffic through a VPN provider or private network; destinations commonly see the VPN egress address.

entities.name: Access control and authentication
entities.description: Mechanisms that restrict access or require proof of authorization.

entities.name: robots.txt
entities.description: A convention for communicating crawler preferences; it is not an access-control mechanism and does not make a URL secret.

entities.name: Browser fingerprinting
entities.description: Using combinations of browser and device characteristics to distinguish or probabilistically recognize clients.

entities.name: HTTP cookies
entities.description: Browser-stored state sent to a site under defined conditions; may support sessions, preferences, or tracking.

entities.name: HTTPS / TLS
entities.description: HTTPS uses TLS to protect HTTP communication between endpoints; it does not hide all connection metadata from all observers.

entities.name: Internet service provider (ISP)
entities.description: An organization providing Internet connectivity; it may observe connection metadata depending on network configuration and encryption.

entities.name: Network observer
entities.description: An entity able to observe some portion of network traffic, such as an ISP, Wi-Fi operator, hosting provider, or state-level observer.

entities.name: Privacy threat model
entities.description: An explicit description of what information must be protected, from which observers, and under what assumptions.

entities.name: Surface web / deep web / dark web distinction
entities.description: A conceptual framework distinguishing indexed content, non-indexed content, and content hosted on anonymity-oriented networks.

attributes.caveat: These labels describe overlapping dimensions rather than perfectly disjoint physical layers.

entities.name: Clearnet versus darknet
entities.description: A terminology contrast between ordinary public Internet services and services reached through specialized anonymity networks.

dimensions.name: accessibility
dimensions.description: Whether a resource can be reached without credentials or specialized network software.

dimensions.name: indexability
dimensions.description: Whether conventional search engines can discover and retrieve a resource.

dimensions.name: network_path
dimensions.description: The route used to reach a destination.

dimensions.name: privacy_linkability
dimensions.description: How readily activity can be linked to a user; depends on multiple signals and the threat model.

ordinary_clearnet_request_flow.action: The user initiates a request to a public website.
Packets are forwarded toward the destination; network operators may observe some connection metadata.
A hostname may be resolved to an IP address; resolver visibility depends on resolver and transport configuration.
Traffic reaches hosting, CDN, reverse-proxy, or origin infrastructure.
TLS protects application traffic in transit between TLS endpoints, but does not conceal all metadata from every observer.
The service processes the request and may receive source address, cookies, account state, and request data.
Operators may log or correlate requests subject to configuration, policy, and law.

anonymity_network_flow.action: The client connects using anonymity-network software.
The entry relay sees the client connection but ordinarily does not know the final destination when Tor is correctly used.
Traffic is forwarded through the circuit.
Public Internet traffic may leave through an exit relay; onion services use Tor's onion-service mechanisms rather than a conventional public-Internet exit.
The destination generally sees the exit address for public-web traffic or the Tor-mediated connection for an onion service, not the client's ordinary public IP.

caveats: These are conceptual flows, not packet-level protocol specifications.
Exact routing depends on the network, protocol, DNS setup, browser, and destination type.
Anonymity networks do not guarantee immunity from endpoint compromise, account-based identification, user disclosure, configuration mistakes, or traffic correlation.

similarities: Often used interchangeably in casual terminology.
differences: Clearnet may mean the public Internet broadly; surface web more specifically means indexed web content.

similarities: Both may be absent from ordinary search-engine results.
differences: Deep web is defined mainly by non-indexing and can include ordinary database portals; dark web usually refers to services hosted on anonymity-oriented networks.

similarities: Both can improve aspects of security or privacy.
differences: HTTPS protects traffic content between endpoints; an anonymity network changes routing and may reduce destination visibility of a client's network address. Neither alone guarantees anonymity.

similarities: Both can affect what address a destination sees.
differences: A VPN generally routes traffic through one provider's egress infrastructure; Tor uses a multi-relay anonymity network. Their trust models and protections differ.

potentially_observable_data: source IP address as seen by a destination or intermediary
request metadata available at relevant endpoints
browser/device characteristics that contribute to fingerprinting
DNS or connection metadata visible to relevant network operators
caveats: Not every website collects or retains every listed data type.
An observed IP address may belong to a shared gateway, VPN, proxy, mobile carrier NAT, or other intermediary.
HTTPS reduces exposure of application content to passive network observers but does not prevent the destination from seeing the request.
Privacy depends on observer position, endpoint security, configuration, provider practices, and legal environment.
threat_model_questions: Which party is the user trying to hide information from: destination website, ISP, local Wi-Fi operator, advertiser, employer, or state-level observer?
Is the goal to hide content, IP address, identity, location, or browsing relationships?
Is the user logged into an identifying account?
Can the endpoint and browser be trusted?
What metadata remains visible at each network hop?
